title: Raise prices plan by plan, with proof of added value
decision_task: Whether and how to raise list prices, especially on popular or unlimited plans, without losing price-sensitive customers.
applies_when: Prices unchanged while value or costs rose
Unlimited or flat top plan attracts heavy users
Owner considers a single large increase
exclusions: Diagnosis points to weak value, delivery or communication (fix those first, BK02)
Existing contracts forbid changes before renewal
No record of added value to explain the change
required_inputs: Owner authorisation and a reviewed migration plan for existing customers
evidence_requirements: Revenue and customer counts per plan
Variable cost per plan, incl. heavy users
Changelog of value added since last price change
Price thresholds relevant to the segment
missing_data_behavior: No value record since the last price: build the case first; no increase yet.
Churn sensitivity unknown: show break-even churn; ask the owner to judge.
alternatives_when_constrained: Low volume: apply to new customers first and observe
No cost data: raise on new customers only and add a fair-use clause
Thin evidence: small steps tied to product improvements (BK02 Ch 12)

decision_branches.if: Value, delivery or communication is the problem
Unlimited or flat top plan attracts heavy users
decision_branches.then: Change limits before a large price jump.
Raise the core plan for new buyers first; existing customers only with notice and owner authorisation.

implementation_steps: Decide new-customer vs existing-customer scope separately
Raise most on the plan with the most demonstrated value; protect the entry price below a key threshold
For unlimited plans, prefer adjusting usage limits or adding a usage component over a very large jump
Compute the churn level at which revenue and contribution break even
Announce with the value record and adequate notice
Monitor churn and downgrades by plan against the break-even
metrics: Churn and downgrade rate vs break-even
guardrails: Existing customers get advance notice per terms; no silent changes
Not a pricing test (PB-pricing-test keeps existing terms unchanged)
observation_window: One renewal cycle for existing customers; 8–12 weeks of new signups.
stop_conditions: Churn exceeds the computed break-even: pause and review
Conversion of new customers falls sharply: reconsider level or packaging
review_triggers: Owner corrects an input this playbook relies on
A metric or guardrail crosses its bound
The underlying source or platform rule changes
climbos_location: New playbook candidate (PB-price-increase, proposed) beside PB-capacity, whose signature currently captures 'price increase' only as a capacity response; plan engine economics stage; calculator for break-even churn.
extends_existing: shared/playbooks/contracts.ts PB-capacity (price increase as a capacity response)

interpretation: Interpretation: the cases show segmentation (protect entry price, raise the core plan, tie to value) and suggest limit changes beat large jumps on unlimited plans; no outcomes were reported, so these are patterns, not proof.
proposed_climbos_rule: Proposed ClimbOS rule: any price-increase recommendation shows per-plan increases, the break-even churn, scope (new vs existing), required notice and the value record; increases on unlimited plans first consider limit or usage changes.
disagreements: PB-pricing-test forbids changing existing customers' terms; a price increase is a separate, owner-authorised migration, not a test. 02_monetization requires a reviewed migration plan, consistent with this rule.

hypothetical_evaluation_cases.label: hypothetical
expected_behavior: Suggests a smaller entry increase that stays below a threshold and a larger core-plan increase if value supports it
Separates new vs existing customers and requires notice
hard_failure: Applying the PricingSaaS 20% average as a recommended increase
Raising existing customers' prices without notice

notes: Proposed reference contract. Not executable; does not authorize publishing, sending or spending. Numbers in source references are dated author figures, never forecasts.
